story: Night-vision lenses so thin and light that we can all see in the dark
text: If you want to learn more ... Vertasium has a good video on the 3-different types of Night Vision. [VIDEO] 1. image intensification 2. active illumination 3. thermal imaging

I watched this video a month ago that might explain it: [VIDEO] . Basically it said infrared goggles use digital processing, so there's at least one frame of lag for every image, which can cause those issues. Image intensifying googles are totally analog so there's no lag to avoid that issue.

story: Apple Vision Pro review: magic, until it's not
text: In case anyone else finds this interesting, the DOD has night vision goggles which have nearly-zero latency (all analog), amplify much better than digital cameras, and emit very little external light (hard to spot by adversaries). This veritasium video at 12:00 shows how these goggles work: [VIDEO] That said I wouldn't be surprised if someone in the DOD was buying them for general tech exploration though.

story: Car insurance in America is too cheap
text: [VIDEO] There are three types of night vision, and the consumer grade active illumination stuff using infrared light is covered by EAR (Department of Commerce’s Export Administration Regulations) instead of ITAR (which is still significant, but less strict). Which doesn't detract from your point, which is that night vision is hamstrung by regulations. With all the advances in technology, the consumer grade stuff should really be more accessible because it would save lives if drivers could see better in the dark.
